RESP grant catch-up: unused room still needs a workable calendar

Five graphics distinguish basic CESG catch-up, annual capacity, the age-16/17 history test and separate lifetime grant and contribution limits.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore basic CESG catch-up under a simplified contribution history

Interactive planning lab

New basic CESG over the modeled calendar years$5,000
New contributions placed within the lifetime limit$25,000
CESG lifetime headroom after the age-17 year$200

Simplified hypothetical history with basic CESG only. Assume Canadian residence and basic eligibility from birth through the calendar year of age 17, valid SIN and promoter arrangements, and no other RESP transactions. The selected earlier contribution years are capped at the number of prior calendar years and placed in the earliest such years, with CAD 2,500 per year and no withdrawals. Earlier basic grants are CAD 500 per funded year, capped at the CAD 7,200 lifetime maximum; no additional CESG was ever received. Unused basic room therefore starts at CAD 500 times prior calendar years less earlier grants. Each modeled year adds CAD 500 of basic room. New grants are 20% of placed contributions, subject to available room, CAD 1,000 per year, the shared lifetime CESG cap and the special pre-age-16 contribution-history condition. New contributions stop at the CAD 50,000 lifetime total; excess requests are unplaced. Delayed years still accrue basic room. No investment return, additional CESG, CLB, provincial benefit, transfer, withdrawal, repayment of grants, real account eligibility or payment-processing lag is calculated. Unused room after age 17 does not extend the grant deadline.

The central idea

Unused grant room is only one constraint. Contributions, annual grant capacity, earlier contribution history and the calendar-year deadline must work together.

01

Distinguish a contribution from a basic grant

The Government of Canada’s CESG guide explains the basic 20% grant, ordinary annual capacity of CAD 500 and catch-up capacity of up to CAD 1,000 when unused room exists. The lifetime CESG limit is CAD 7,200 per beneficiary, including any additional CESG.

The fixed reference chart compares grant dollars on CAD 1,000, CAD 2,500 and CAD 5,000 of contributions. With sufficient unused room and all other conditions met, CAD 5,000 can attract CAD 1,000 of basic CESG. Without earlier unused room, that larger contribution does not double the ordinary CAD 500 grant.

The grant is separate from the family’s contribution and is not an investment return. This model excludes additional CESG, the Canada Learning Bond and provincial benefits. It assumes basic eligibility and Canadian residence throughout the relevant calendar years.

02

Make the simplified earlier history explicit

The default begins in the calendar year the beneficiary turns thirteen. Four earlier calendar years each received CAD 2,500 of contributions. The scenario places those funded years at the beginning of the child’s calendar-year history, with no withdrawals or other RESP transactions.

That creates CAD 10,000 of prior family contributions and CAD 2,000 of prior basic CESG. Thirteen prior eligible calendar years accumulated CAD 6,500 of basic room, so CAD 4,500 remains unused before the first new year.

The earlier-years control is capped at the number of prior calendar years. This is a deliberately constructed history, not an account reconstruction. Real records may include different amounts, residency periods, other subscribers, additional grants or grant repayments, requiring a promoter’s reconciliation.

03

Apply the annual and lifetime limits in sequence

The default requests CAD 5,000 each year from the year turning thirteen through the year turning seventeen. Each year first adds CAD 500 of new basic room, then applies that year’s contribution and the grant constraints.

The five new grants are CAD 1,000 each, producing CAD 5,000 of new basic CESG. Prior plus new grants total CAD 7,000, leaving CAD 200 of lifetime grant headroom. Family contributions total CAD 35,000, including the earlier CAD 10,000.

The CRA’s contribution-limit page sets a separate CAD 50,000 lifetime contribution ceiling across all RESPs for the beneficiary. Grants do not consume that contribution ceiling. This tool leaves requests above remaining contribution capacity unplaced and does not create an excess contribution.

04

Check the special history condition before ages sixteen and seventeen

The government’s grant guide requires an earlier contribution history for CESG at ages sixteen and seventeen: by the end of the calendar year turning fifteen, either CAD 2,000 must have been contributed and not withdrawn, or at least CAD 100 in each of four years.

The model tracks both tests. Its earlier CAD 2,500 years satisfy the first condition whenever at least one exists. Without earlier funded years, new contributions through the year turning fifteen can establish a qualifying history.

For example, change the start age to sixteen and earlier funded years to zero. A new contribution is still placed within the model’s RESP capacity, but no basic CESG is credited: a current contribution cannot repair a missed pre-sixteen condition. The tool assumes no withdrawals that would undo that history.

05

Read unused room alongside the remaining calendar

Unused basic room in the default remains CAD 2,000 at the end, even though lifetime grant headroom is only CAD 200. These numbers describe different constraints. Neither permits a new CESG after the end of the calendar year turning seventeen.

The matrix waits zero to three years before starting the annual requests. A two-year delay leaves only the years turning fifteen, sixteen and seventeen in the default history. Even a larger annual request cannot bypass the annual grant ceiling.

Compare the contribution budget with verified records and remaining eligible years. No return, tax deduction, education withdrawal or payment-processing lag is included. The charts explain timing and limits; they do not confirm an actual grant award or recommend using education savings ahead of other household needs.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. The first graphic applies published basic CESG rules to fixed reference contributions. The other graphics use a simplified hypothetical history with no additional CESG, rather than a verified child’s entitlement. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. Government of Canada · RESP benefit amounts and CESG carry-forward ↗

    Reviewed 25 October 2026, including the expanded age-16/17 and carry-forward sections. Supports the basic grant rate, annual constraints, lifetime CESG ceiling and contribution-history deadline. The model excludes all additional CESG and assumes eligibility from birth; its earlier contribution pattern is hypothetical.

  2. CRA · Registered Education Savings Plans contributions ↗

    Reviewed 25 October 2026 for the separate lifetime contribution limit across plans and treatment of government incentives. The scenario caps contributions instead of modeling excesses, and does not determine actual available capacity from private records.
